overview: Hyperthyroidism occurs when the thyroid gland produces too much thyroid hormone (T3 and T4), speeding up the body's metabolism and causing a range of symptoms.

types.name: Graves' Disease
types.description: Most common cause. An autoimmune disorder causing the thyroid to overproduce hormones.

types.name: Toxic Multinodular Goiter
types.description: Multiple nodules in thyroid produce excess hormones independently.

types.name: Thyroiditis
types.description: Inflammation releasing stored hormones — can be temporary.

types.name: Excessive Iodine Intake
types.description: Too much iodine (from diet or medications) triggers overproduction.

symptoms: Unintentional weight loss despite increased appetite
diagnosis: TSH (Thyroid Stimulating Hormone) Test — low in hyperthyroidism
Free T4 and T3 levels — elevated

medications: Radioactive iodine therapy (RAI) — destroys overactive thyroid cells
surgical: Thyroidectomy (partial or total removal) — for large goiters or failed medical therapy
lifestyle: Avoid iodine-rich foods (seaweed, iodized salt in excess)
Adequate calcium and vitamin D intake (post-surgery)

prevention: Regular thyroid screenings if at risk
emergency_signs: Thyroid storm: fever > 103°F, rapid heart rate, confusion, vomiting

faqs.question: Can hyperthyroidism be cured?
faqs.answer: Yes, with radioactive iodine therapy or surgery, hyperthyroidism can be permanently cured, though hypothyroidism may follow and require lifelong hormone replacement.

faqs.question: Is hyperthyroidism dangerous?
faqs.answer: Untreated hyperthyroidism can lead to serious complications like heart disease, bone loss, and thyroid storm. With proper treatment, it is manageable.
